newsitem.title: FRANCE: SOCCER-ITALIANS NEXT IN LINE FOR ROBERTO CARLOS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-ITALIANS NEXT IN LINE FOR ROBERTO CARLOS.

text.p: Italian goalkeepers Angelo Peruzzi and Gianluca Pagluica gave no hint of fear on Friday -- but they could be forgiven for quaking in their boots.

Because one of them -- and even possibly both if one is substituted suffering from shellshock -- could be next to face one of Roberto Carlos's blistering freekicks which made headlines around the world on Tuesday.
The 35-metre shot, which swerved out and around the French wall timed at 137 kph and gave Brazil the lead against France in Lyon, is already being talked about as one of the best goals ever scored.
With the outside of his left foot, Roberto Carlos swerved the ball so far wide of the wall that a ball-boy five metres left of the French goal ducked because he thought it was going to hit him.
It needed television pictures and the camera angle behind the shot to show just how remarkable a goal it was.

Roberto Carlos took a 10-metre run-up and sent the ball flying four metres wide to the left of the last defender in the French wall before whipping back like a boomerang and going in off a post. French goalkeeper Fabien Barthez looked on in stunned amazement as the ball sped past him.
Now the Italians, who play Brazil in their next match in the Tournoi de France in Lyon on Sunday, are in the firing line.
Pagliuca knows all about Real Madrid's Roberto Carlos from the time they spent together at Inter Milan.
"He's a Brazilian," said Pagliuca as if that explained everything there was to know about the goal.

"There is nothing you can do with a shot like that. You could put another man in the wall but if he hit it well it would still go in. He used to do it all the time in training but even though you know what's coming, you can't stop them."

Fellow 'keeper Angelo Peruzzi said: "It was a really great goal, an incredible goal, he hit it just right. What's the secret of a shot like that? Well, I don't know. Even if you put more players in the wall to stop it on the left side, he could bend it round the other way and he'll catch you there."
The day after the goal newspapers and magazines around the world printed diagrams of what had happened --- and rival players took to the training pitch to try to emulate it.

England's Stuart Pearce, a noted free-kick expert who has scored some stunning goals himself from around the box including one for Nottingham Forest in the 1991 F.A. Cup Final, said: "It was a wonder goal, one of the best goals I have ever seen. It was an absolutely wonderful strike.
"We were all out on the training pitch the next morning trying to swerve it like that -- but we ended up losing a few balls down the motorway," he joked.

His team mate David Beckham, who scored from inside his own half for Manchester United against Wimbledon on the first day of the season and also scored with a memorable swerving shot of his own against Tottenham in January, added: "It was some run-up, wasn't it? I think I would break my foot if I hit it like that to be honest."
The French were no less impressed. Barthez blamed himself for positioning the wall badly -- but he would have had to have erected one with watch-towers and guard-dogs to have stopped the goal.
"Once the ball was hit it was too late and I think the goal was my fault. But it was a superb strike and just too fast for me."

Bruno N'Gotty, who scored with a devastating drive from a short-range freekick to win the 1996 European Cup Winners' Cup for Paris St Germain said: "Many can attempt a shot like that -- but they don't dare."
And what about Roberto Carlos himself? He says if he uses the inside of his left foot, he can make the ball fly over he wall and then dip down under the crossbar.
"I scored one like that for Real Madrid against Celta in the League this season," he explained, "It went over the wall and dipped down sharply."
As if Peruzzi and Pagliuca did not have enough to worry about already.
